name: Sūrya (as revealer of jyotiṣa)
summary: The Sun as the source of astronomical knowledge: he taught the Sūrya Siddhānta to the asura Maya through a person born of his own portion (SS 1.4–9); he granted Varāhamihira a boon at Kāpitthaka (BJ 28.9); in horā he is the self (ātman) of the Kālapuruṣa (BJ 2.1) and the lord of planets to whom Parāśara bows (BPHS 1.6).

name: Maya (the asura)
summary: The great asura who, when little of the Kṛta age remained, performed hard austerities to the Sun wishing to know the Vedāṅga of the lights, and received the Sūrya Siddhānta from a person born of the Sun's portion (SS 1.2–9; 12.1–11).

name: Brahmā (as source of jyotiṣa)
summary: In jyotiṣa, Pitāmaha is the source of the Paitāmaha Siddhānta; Āryabhaṭa says his knowledge was raised from the ocean of true and false knowledge by Brahmā's grace (Āryabhaṭīya 4.49); Parāśara teaches the horā 'as heard from Brahmā's mouth' (BPHS 1.6); Brahmā granted Rāhu the boon of receiving the offerings made at eclipses (BS 5.14).

name: Parāśara (as teacher of horā)
summary: For jyotiṣa, the seer who teaches the horā to Maitreya in the Bṛhat Parāśara Horā Śāstra (tradition's account; the text is a late compilation by scholarly account). Varāhamihira already cites Parāśara among earlier authorities (BJ 12.2 on the mālā and sarpa yogas); the commentators take 'Śaktipūrva' in BJ 7.1 as Parāśara, Śakti's son.

name: Maitreya (Parāśara's questioner)
summary: In the Bṛhat Parāśara Horā Śāstra, the sage who approaches Parāśara with folded hands and asks for the horā, best of the three branches of jyotiṣa (BPHS 1.1–3).

name: Jaimini (as author of the Upadeśa Sūtras)
summary: For jyotiṣa, the seer to whom the tradition ascribes the Upadeśa Sūtras of the Jaimini system (sign-aspects, cara-kārakas, cara-daśā), identified by the tradition with the author of the Mīmāṃsā Sūtra; commentators say he composed it at Kāśī. Scholarly account: date and authorship uncertain.

name: Garga (as teacher of saṃhitā)
summary: For jyotiṣa, the ancient sage whose saṃhitā on omens and lunar mansions (Vṛddhagargasaṃhitā) is the principal older source of Varāhamihira's saṃhitā; Varāhamihira says he will relate the portents that Garga taught to Atri (BS 45.1).

name: Vasiṣṭha (as jyotiṣa authority)
summary: One of the promulgators of jyotiṣa: the Vāsiṣṭha Siddhānta (summarized in the Pañcasiddhāntikā) and a Vasiṣṭha Saṃhitā on muhūrta are ascribed to him.

name: Nārada (as jyotiṣa authority)
summary: Among the promulgators of jyotiṣa; a Nārada Saṃhitā on muhūrta and omens is ascribed to him, and the Nārada Purāṇa contains a section on the three branches of jyotiṣa.

name: Bhṛgu (as jyotiṣa authority)
summary: The seer to whom the Bhṛgu Saṃhitā — held to contain the horoscopes of all persons — and the Bhṛgusūtra on house results are ascribed.

name: Agastya (in jyotiṣa and the nāḍīs)
summary: The seer whose star's heliacal rising (Agastyacāra, BS 12) is a saṃhitā topic, and the most cited author of the Tamil palm-leaf nāḍīs (the tradition's claim).

name: Puliśa
summary: The author to whom the Pauliśa Siddhānta is ascribed; known through Varāhamihira and later citations. Historicity unknown.

name: Yavanācārya ('the Yavana teacher')
summary: The teacher or teachers called 'the Yavanas' whom Varāhamihira cites on longevity (BJ 7.1), royal yogas (BJ 11.1) and the count of nābhasa yogas (BJ 12.1), and whom he says are honoured like seers (BS 2.14).

name: Yavaneśvara
summary: The 'lord of the Yavanas' who, by the Yavanajātaka's own closing account (as read by Pingree), rendered a Greek horoscopic text into Sanskrit prose in 149/150 CE.

name: Sphujidhvaja
summary: Author of the versified Yavanajātaka (269/270 CE by Pingree's reading).

name: Mīnarāja
summary: Author of the Vṛddhayavanajātaka, a large versified horā in the Yavana tradition.

name: Satya (Satyācārya)
summary: An earlier horā teacher whose method of longevity Varāhamihira prefers: 'Satya's teaching is best here' (BJ 7.13); also cited on the drekkāṇas.
notes: Known only from citations in Varāhamihira and his commentators.

name: Maṇittha
summary: An earlier authority on longevity named by Varāhamihira with Maya, the Yavanas and Śaktipūrva (BJ 7.1).
notes: Known only from citations in Varāhamihira and his commentators.

name: Jīvaśarman
summary: An earlier horā teacher whose own views on longevity (BJ 7.9) and royal yogas (BJ 11.1) Varāhamihira reports.
notes: Known only from citations in Varāhamihira and his commentators.

name: Viṣṇugupta (as horā author)
summary: Named with Devasvāmin and Siddhasena as having taught a longevity method (BJ 7.7); later tradition sometimes identifies him with Cāṇakya (identification uncertain).
notes: Known only from citations in Varāhamihira and his commentators.

name: Devasvāmin
summary: Horā author named by Varāhamihira among those who taught longevity (BJ 7.7).
notes: Known only from citations in Varāhamihira and his commentators.

name: Siddhasena (as horā author)
summary: Horā author named by Varāhamihira among those who taught longevity (BJ 7.7); not to be assumed identical with the Jain logician Siddhasena Divākara.
notes: Known only from citations in Varāhamihira and his commentators.

name: Āryabhaṭa
summary: Author of the Āryabhaṭīya, written when he was 23 in the year 3600 of the Kali age (499 CE) and honoured at Kusumapura. He taught the equal quarters of the yuga, the rotation of the earth (the boat simile), eclipses by the earth's shadow and the moon, and an alphabetic numeral notation; he opens by bowing to Ka, the supreme Brahman, and says his knowledge came by Brahmā's grace. His school (āryapakṣa) dominated South India and Kerala; Brahmagupta criticized him for departing from the smṛti.

name: Varāhamihira
summary: The great compiler of all three branches of jyotiṣa: Pañcasiddhāntikā (siddhānta), Bṛhajjātaka and Laghujātaka (horā), Bṛhat Saṃhitā (saṃhitā), and works on marriage and royal expeditions (Yogayātrā). Son and pupil of Ādityadāsa, of Avanti, he received a boon from the Sun at Kāpitthaka and composed his horā after studying the views of the seers (BJ 28.9); he bows to the former promulgators (BJ 28.10) and honours the Yavanas (BS 2.14). Tradition counts him among the 'nine jewels' of Vikramāditya's court (scholarly account: a later legend).

scholarly.text: 6th c. CE; Pañcasiddhāntikā epoch 505; death 587 by a late report

realization_account.text: Received a boon of grace from the Sun (savitṛ-labdha-vara-prasāda) at Kāpitthaka.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

name: Ādityadāsa
summary: Father and teacher of Varāhamihira, from whom he received his knowledge (BJ 28.9).

name: Pṛthuyaśas
summary: Son of Varāhamihira by tradition; author of the Horāsāra and the Ṣaṭpañcāśikā on interrogation.

name: Bhāskara I
summary: Expositor of the Āryabhaṭa school: Mahābhāskarīya, Laghubhāskarīya and the commentary on the Āryabhaṭīya (629 CE).

name: Brahmagupta
summary: Son of Jiṣṇu, astronomer of Bhillamāla; author of the Brāhmasphuṭasiddhānta (628, at age 30) and the Khaṇḍakhādyaka (665). He upheld the smṛti's yuga proportions and the stationary earth against Āryabhaṭa; founder figure of the Brāhma school.

name: Lalla
summary: Author of the Śiṣyadhīvṛddhida in the Āryabhaṭa school.

name: Haridatta
summary: Kerala astronomer credited with the Parahita system (683 CE) correcting the Āryabhaṭa constants.

name: Pṛthūdakasvāmin
summary: Commentator on the Brāhmasphuṭasiddhānta and Khaṇḍakhādyaka (864 CE).

name: Bhaṭṭotpala
summary: The great commentator on Varāhamihira's works (Bṛhajjātaka, Bṛhat Saṃhitā, Laghujātaka, Yogayātrā) and on Pṛthuyaśas; his commentaries preserve many lost earlier texts.

name: Vaṭeśvara
summary: Author of the Vaṭeśvarasiddhānta (904 CE), defender of the Āryabhaṭa school.

name: Mañjula (Muñjāla)
summary: Author of the Laghumānasa (932 CE); later authors credit him with a theory of the motion of the solstices (ayana-calana).

name: Śrīpati
summary: 11th-century author of the Siddhāntaśekhara, the Jyotiṣaratnamālā on muhūrta and a manual (paddhati) of nativities with his method of house division.

name: Śatānanda
summary: Author of the Bhāsvatī (1099 CE), a Sūrya-Siddhānta-based handbook for calendars, traditionally of Puri.

name: Mahāvīrācārya
summary: Jain mathematician, author of the Gaṇitasārasaṅgraha under the Rāṣṭrakūṭa king Amoghavarṣa.

name: Bhāskara II (Bhāskarācārya)
summary: Born Śaka 1036 (1114 CE), son and pupil of Maheśvara; author of the Siddhānta Śiromaṇi (1150) with Līlāvatī, Bījagaṇita, Grahagaṇita and Golādhyāya, and the Karaṇakutūhala (1183). He taught that the earth rests in space by its own power and has a power of attraction.

name: Kalyāṇavarman
summary: Author of the Sārāvalī, a large compendium of horā; described as a king of Vyāghrataṭī (low confidence).

name: Mantreśvara
summary: Author of the Phaladīpikā; South Indian (tradition places him in the Tamil country). Dates uncertain.

name: Vaidyanātha Dīkṣita
summary: Author of the Jātakapārijāta.

name: Veṅkaṭeśa Daivajña
summary: Author of the Sarvārthacintāmaṇi.

name: Ḍhuṇḍhirāja
summary: Author of the Jātakābharaṇa.

name: Gaṇeśa (author of the Jātakālaṅkāra)
summary: Author of the Jātakālaṅkāra (1613); distinct from Gaṇeśa Daivajña.

name: Nārāyaṇa Bhaṭṭa (author of the Camatkāracintāmaṇi)
summary: Author of the Camatkāracintāmaṇi on house results.

name: Kālidāsa (as ascribed author of the Uttarakālāmṛta)
summary: The Kālidāsa to whom the Uttarakālāmṛta is ascribed; the tradition sometimes identifies him with the poet (doubtful), as it also ascribes to 'Kālidāsa' the Jyotirvidābharaṇa.

name: Keśava Daivajña
summary: Astronomer-astrologer of Nandigrāma, father and teacher of Gaṇeśa Daivajña; author of the Jātakapaddhati and of observational corrections (Grahakautuka).

name: Gaṇeśa Daivajña
summary: Son and pupil of Keśava, of Nandigrāma; author of the Grahalāghava (1520), the basis of many almanacs.

name: Ananta Daivajña
summary: Astrologer of a family settled at Kāśī, father of Nīlakaṇṭha and Rāma Daivajña (MC 1.2 names Rāma as Ananta's son).

name: Rāma Daivajña
summary: Son of Ananta, younger brother of Nīlakaṇṭha; author of the Muhūrtacintāmaṇi (Kāśī, 1600) with his own commentary.

name: Nīlakaṇṭha Daivajña
summary: Son of Ananta; author of the Tājikanīlakaṇṭhī (1587), the standard Tājika text; associated by tradition with the court of Akbar.

name: Govinda Daivajña
summary: Son of Nīlakaṇṭha Daivajña; author of the Pīyūṣadhārā commentary on the Muhūrtacintāmaṇi (1603).

name: Nārāyaṇa (author of the Muhūrtamārtaṇḍa)
summary: Author of the Muhūrtamārtaṇḍa (1571).

name: Balabhadra
summary: 17th-century compiler of the Horāratna and the Hāyanaratna on Tājika.

name: Kamalākara (astronomer)
summary: Astronomer of Kāśī, author of the Siddhāntatattvaviveka (1658) in defence of the Saura school; distinct from Kamalākara Bhaṭṭa of the Nirṇayasindhu.

name: Raṅganātha (commentator on the Sūrya Siddhānta)
summary: Author of the Gūḍhārthaprakāśa on the Sūrya Siddhānta (1603).

name: Samarasiṃha
summary: Author of one of the earliest Sanskrit Tājika works (1274).

name: Hemaprabha
summary: Jain author of the Trailokyaprakāśa (1248) on Tājika and horā.

name: Ballālasena
summary: Sena king of Bengal who began the Adbhutasāgara, a digest of omens (1168), completed by his son Lakṣmaṇasena.

name: Vasantarāja
summary: Author of the Vasantarāja Śākuna on augury.

name: Vidyāraṇya / Mādhavācārya (as author on time)
summary: The Mādhavācārya to whom the Kālamādhava on the right times of rites is ascribed; the tradition identifies him with Vidyāraṇya.

name: Mādhava of Saṅgamagrāma
summary: Founder figure of the Kerala school of astronomy and mathematics; teacher of Parameśvara.

name: Parameśvara (of Vaṭaśśeri)
summary: Kerala astronomer who observed for over fifty years and composed the Dṛggaṇita (1431), the Goladīpikā and commentaries on the Āryabhaṭīya and Sūrya Siddhānta.

name: Nīlakaṇṭha Somayājī
summary: Kerala astronomer (a Somayājin Nambūtiri), author of the Tantrasaṅgraha (1500) and a large commentary on the Āryabhaṭīya; pupil of Dāmodara, son of Parameśvara.

name: Jyeṣṭhadeva
summary: Author of the Malayalam Yuktibhāṣā setting out the demonstrations of the Kerala school.

name: Acyuta Piṣāraṭi
summary: Kerala astronomer, pupil of Jyeṣṭhadeva and teacher of Nārāyaṇa Bhaṭṭatiri (author of the Nārāyaṇīyam).

name: Govinda Bhaṭṭatiri
summary: Kerala astrologer to whom the Daśādhyāyī commentary on the Bṛhajjātaka is ascribed; celebrated in Kerala legend.

name: Rudra (Kerala commentator)
summary: Author of the Vivaraṇa commentary on the Bṛhajjātaka preserved in Kerala manuscripts.

name: Anavamadarśī (Saṅgharāja)
summary: Sri Lankan monk to whom the Daivajñakāmadhenu, a Sanskrit manual of jyotiṣa, is ascribed.

name: Jagannātha Samrāṭ
summary: Astronomer of Sawai Jai Singh II who rendered Arabic versions of Ptolemy (Samrāṭ Siddhānta, 1732) and Euclid into Sanskrit.

name: Sawai Jai Singh II
summary: Rājput king of Amber/Jaipur who built masonry observatories at Delhi, Jaipur, Ujjain, Varanasi and Mathura and sponsored astronomical tables.

name: Bāpudeva Śāstrī
summary: Professor of astronomy at the Sanskrit College, Benares; worked on almanac (pañcāṅga) reform and wrote Sanskrit works on astronomy.

name: Sāmanta Candraśekhara
summary: Odia astronomer who, with naked-eye instruments of his own making, corrected planetary constants within the siddhānta framework in the Siddhāntadarpaṇa.

name: Sudhākara Dvivedī
summary: Benares scholar who edited the Brāhmasphuṭasiddhānta and other siddhāntas and wrote the Gaṇakataraṅgiṇī on the lives of Indian astronomers.

name: B. V. Raman
summary: Bangalore astrologer and editor of The Astrological Magazine; wrote widely in English on horā and muhūrta and proposed his own ayanāṃśa.

name: K. S. Krishnamurti
summary: Founder of the Krishnamurti Paddhati (KP), which subdivides each nakṣatra by the proportions of the Viṃśottarī periods into 'sub-lords'.

name: N. C. Lahiri
summary: Calcutta astronomer-almanac maker whose ayanāṃśa (the Citrāpakṣa, with Spica at 180°) was adopted for the Indian national ephemeris after the Calendar Reform Committee of the 1950s.

name: Sri Yukteswar (on the yugas)
summary: In The Holy Science (1894) proposed a 24,000-year cycle of ascending and descending yugas, holding that the conventional reckoning of the Kali age was mistaken.
